name: Storm-1113
keyCapabilities: Automated Data Gathering of System Diagnostics
recommendedActions: Block or restrict the 'ms-appinstaller' protocol handler on internal networks.
Configure EDR policies to alert on 'file pumping' (discrepancy between file size and content length).
Implement web filtering to block known malicious domains and high-risk search result redirects.
Standardize policy against the use of tools like AnyDesk or 3proxy unless officially sanctioned.
Monitor for script execution using vbs_ files in common temporary directories (e.g., \\Windows\\Temp\).
Alert on unusual PowerShell commands involving -w hidden, -enc, and IEX syntax from remote URLs.
Conduct audits of search results for enterprise-used tools like Zoom to detect landing page spoofing.
Ensure timely patching of system components related to signature enforcement (e.g., Defender SmartScreen).
campaignsText: Storm-1113 is a primary driver of the 'Resident' campaign, known for its Russian-speaking operations targeting manufacturing and commerce. They have been active since at least late 2022, frequently collaborating with or providing infrastructure for other 'Storm' clusters like those associated with Sage and various ransomware groups. Their operational tempo involves rapid deployment of landing pages during peak software demand and a high frequency of search result manipulation to drive volume. Notably, their tactics in 2023-2024 led to the wide-scale removal of several Windows installation methods that were being exploited as primary delivery vectors for their tools.
description: Storm-1113 (also known as APOTHECARY SPIDER) functions as a sophisticated access broker and 'as-a-service' provider, specializing in producing malicious infrastructure and loaders to facilitate broad information theft. The group gained significant visibility due to the scale of its delivery tactics—specifically utilizing fraudulent search advertisements and MSIX packages—which were extensive enough to trigger broad changes to Windows security features.
goals: Storm-1113 primarily seeks to monetize access through two avenues: selling access to high-value targets to other cybercriminal groups and profiting from the direct theft of credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, and personal information via 'stealer' malware. Their targeting strategy is expansive rather than precise; they use search engine poisoning (SEO) to target any user searching for popular software, resulting in a broad net cast across commercial, financial, and government sectors.
